# eBPF from Scratch: Watch an Agent, Then Stop It

Write an eBPF program in C, load it from Python with nothing but ctypes and libbpf, and watch a coding agent's process tree name every file it opens and every address it dials. Then kill the agent when it reaches for a credential, deny the open with a BPF LSM hook, and ship every event to an OpenTelemetry collector.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=ebpf-from-scratch&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=ebpf-from-scratch_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

This lab runs its agent on a local Ollama model. The Zenable sandbox has the model already downloaded and built; take the hosted version at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=ebpf-from-scratch&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=ebpf-from-scratch_readme.

**Duration** 45 minutes · **Difficulty** Intermediate

**Topics** `Security` · `Guardrails & Policy` · `Observability`

**Prerequisites**

- The Syscalls and seccomp lab, or comfort with what a system call is
- Ability to read a short C function; you won't write one from nothing
- Python 3.12+ and uv, Docker
- A Linux kernel with BTF and the BPF LSM enabled. Your sandbox has both; the Getting started section checks

---

_This README is only the hands-on lab. The concept walk-through (seccomp decides by number, and the number isn't the story · Terminology · Conclusion) lives on the [Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=ebpf-from-scratch&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=ebpf-from-scratch_readme)._

## One-liners first

_~7 min · Hands-on_

Before writing a program, let's use one somebody already wrote. [bpftrace](https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace) compiles a one-line script into an eBPF program, loads it, and prints what comes back. This one prints every `openat` made by a process named `cat`, with the path:

```bash
sudo timeout 5 bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat /comm == "cat"/ { printf("%s %d %s\n", comm, pid, str(args->filename)); }' &
sleep 1
cat workspace/VERSION >/dev/null
wait
```

```console
$ sudo timeout 5 bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat /comm == "cat"/ { printf("%s %d %s\n", comm, pid, str(args->filename)); }' &
$ sleep 1
Attaching 1 probe...
$ cat workspace/VERSION >/dev/null
cat 9353 /etc/ld.so.cache
cat 9353 /lib64/libc.so.6
cat 9353 /usr/lib/locale/locale-archive
cat 9353 workspace/VERSION
$ wait
```

There's the fact seccomp couldn't see: the filename, read straight out of the calling process's memory by `str(args->filename)`. Now the whole agent, with three hooks at once. `execve` for programs started, `openat` for files, and `connect` with the address decoded:

```bash
sudo bpftrace -e '
tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_execve { printf("exec    %-16s %s\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }
tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat /strncmp(str(args->filename), "decoys", 6) == 0/ { printf("open    %-16s %s\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }
tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_connect /comm == "curl" && args->uservaddr->sa_family == 2/ { printf("connect %-16s %s:%d\n", comm, ntop(((struct sockaddr_in *)args->uservaddr)->sin_addr.s_addr), bswap(((struct sockaddr_in *)args->uservaddr)->sin_port)); }
' > bpftrace.out 2>&1 &
sleep 2
./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
sudo pkill -INT bpftrace; wait
grep -E 'exec .*/(cat|curl)$|open |connect ' bpftrace.out | head -20
```

```console
$ grep -E 'exec .*/(cat|curl)$|open |connect ' bpftrace.out | head -20
```

Success! The first lab's three story lines are back, and this time each one names its object: `cat` opening `decoys/.aws/credentials`, and `curl` connecting to an address on port 443 (after the resolver on port 53). bpftrace saw every process on the machine, not just ours, which is why the `execve` line is filtered to `cat` and `curl` and the `connect` line to `curl`; without that filter the model's own traffic to `127.0.0.1:11434` fills the screen. Attributing events to one agent is the first thing our own program has to do better.

Question: the `connect` hook cast `args->uservaddr` to `struct sockaddr_in` and read the port with `bswap`. Why the byte swap?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Ports and addresses in a `sockaddr_in` are in network byte order, big-endian, and x86_64 is little-endian. `ntop()` knows that for addresses; for the port you swap it yourself or read `11434` as `43308`. It also explains why seccomp could never have done this: the address lives in userspace memory that the filter can't read, and even the raw bytes need decoding before they mean anything.

</details>

## From scratch: the program

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Open `bpf/agentwatch.bpf.c`. It has four hooks, an event ring, and maps for the kill switch and cgroup scope. `bpf/policy.h` shares the scope and credential-path checks with the LSM program. The struct at the top is the wire format for every event, and the Python side unpacks exactly this:

```c
struct event {
    __u32 kind;
    __u32 pid;
    __u32 ppid;
    __u32 uid;
    char comm[COMM_BYTES];
    char data[PATH_MAX_BYTES];
};

struct {
    __uint(type, BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF);
    __uint(max_entries, 1 << 20);
} events SEC(".maps");
```

`SEC(".maps")` tells libbpf to create the ring buffer when the object loads. Each hook is a function with a `SEC()` naming where it attaches, and each emits events by reserving a slot, filling it, and submitting it. The enforcement decision happens first, so a full ring cannot disable it. Here's `openat`:

```c
SEC("tracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_openat")
int on_openat(struct trace_event_raw_sys_enter *ctx)
{
    if (!should_observe())
        return 0;
    char path[PATH_MAX_BYTES] = {};
    const char *filename = (const char *)ctx->args[1];
    bpf_probe_read_user_str(path, sizeof(path), filename);
    int killed = in_scope() && kill_wanted() && is_credential_path(path);
    // Enforcement cannot depend on space in the telemetry ring.
    if (killed)
        bpf_send_signal(SIGKILL);
    struct event *e = reserve(killed ? EVENT_DENIED : EVENT_OPEN);
    if (!e)
        return 0;
    __builtin_memcpy(e->data, path, sizeof(path));
    bpf_ringbuf_submit(e, 0);
    return 0;
}
```

`bpf_probe_read_user_str` is the helper that reads the path out of the calling process's memory, safely, with a bound. That one line is the whole difference from seccomp. Ignore the `kill_wanted` branch for now; it's the next section.

The kernel checks cgroup membership before recording each event. The launcher enrols the command before it can exec, and every fork inherits that membership. Fork events explain the process relationships; enforcement does not depend on receiving every event:

```c
SEC("tracepoint/sched/sched_process_fork")
int on_fork(struct trace_event_raw_sched_process_fork *ctx)
{
    if (!should_observe())
        return 0;
    struct event *e = bpf_ringbuf_reserve(&events, sizeof(*e), 0);
    if (!e)
        return 0;
    __builtin_memset(e, 0, sizeof(*e));
    e->kind = EVENT_FORK;
    e->pid = ctx->child_pid;
    e->ppid = ctx->parent_pid;
    ...
```

Compile it. `make` first dumps the kernel's BTF into `vmlinux.h`, so the `trace_event_raw_*` structs above are this kernel's exact layout, then runs clang with `-target bpf`. The kernel uses tagged anonymous struct members, so we enable [the same C extension as its build](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v7.0/Makefile#L1097) with `-fms-extensions`. Clang may still report extension warnings from the generated header; those stay visible. The build below was captured in an arm64 Linux container; the sandbox uses `__TARGET_ARCH_x86`:

```bash
ls -la bpf/
```

Two object files. Let's see what the kernel will get before we hand it over:

```bash
llvm-objdump -h bpf/agentwatch.bpf.o | grep -E 'tracepoint|lsm|maps'
```

```console
 3 tracepoint/sched/sched_process_fork       000003e8 0000000000000000 TEXT

 6 .reltracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_execve  00000030 0000000000000000

 8 .reltracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_openat  00000050 0000000000000000

10 .reltracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_connect 00000030 0000000000000000
12 .maps                                     00000050 0000000000000000 DATA
```

One ELF section per hook, named after the `SEC()` string, plus `.maps`. That's the contract libbpf reads: it opens the file, creates a map per entry in `.maps`, loads each program section into the kernel (the verifier runs here), and attaches each one to the tracepoint its section name spells out.

Now the Python side. `libbpf.py` declares the libbpf 1.x functions we need through `ctypes`, and `agentwatch.py` uses them in the order just described:

```python
with libbpf.Object(str(WATCH_OBJ)) as watch:
    watch.load()
    with process_scope.create() as scope:
        libbpf.map_set_u64(watch.map_fd("scope_config"), 0, scope.stat().st_ino)
        libbpf.map_set_u32(watch.map_fd("watch_config"), 0, int(args.kill))
        watch.attach_all()

        def on_record(record: bytes) -> None:
            print(render(decode(record)), flush=True)

        with libbpf.Ring(watch.map_fd("events"), on_record) as ring:
            child = process_scope.launch(command, scope)
            try:
                while child.poll() is None:
                    ring.poll(100)
            finally:
                process_scope.stop(scope)
                child.wait()
```

The scope map is populated before attachment. `process_scope.launch` starts an isolated helper that drops to the invoking user, enrols it in the root-owned cgroup, then releases it to exec the command. Its descendants inherit the scope even if a fork event is lost. On normal exit, exceptions, SIGINT, or SIGTERM, the loader kills the cgroup's remaining processes before destroying the BPF links. `--all` expands observation to the machine; enforcement still targets only this cgroup.

This requires cgroup v2 and `cgroup.kill` (Linux 5.14 or later). On a host using v1 controllers, the loader mounts a controller-free v2 hierarchy for the run and removes its mount on exit. It does not migrate the host's resource controllers. This is a teaching policy for unprivileged commands: a command that gains root can change its cgroup or the BPF policy.

Run `task test` in a fresh clone for the portable tests and notebook. On the Linux sandbox, `sudo task test KERNEL=true` also compiles and loads the programs, checks that unrelated processes remain unaffected, fills the event ring, and tests descendant cleanup. This mode fails if the required kernel facilities or toolchain are missing.

Run it:

```bash
sudo uv run python agentwatch.py -- ./run-agent.sh > agentwatch.out 2>&1
grep -E '^(exec|open|connect|fork)' agentwatch.out | grep -E 'cat|curl|decoys|:443|:11434' | head -20
```

```console
$ sudo uv run python agentwatch.py -- ./run-agent.sh > agentwatch.out 2>&1
$ grep -E '^(exec|open|connect|fork)' agentwatch.out | grep -E 'cat|curl|decoys|:443|:11434' | head -20
```

Success! Same facts as bpftrace, but now every line carries a pid and a parent pid, and there is nothing from any other process on the machine. That's a program you wrote deciding what the kernel tells you.

Question: `open` lines from goose itself reference files under `goose/state/` and the model's `config.yaml`. Which of those would you want a sandbox to allow, and which to flag? There's no answer panel for this one; hold it for the next lab, where a policy has to say.

## Stop it

_~8 min · Hands-on_

Watching was step one. `--kill` flips the config map so `on_openat` sends `SIGKILL` to any process in the tree that opens a path containing `/.aws/`:

```bash
sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --kill -- ./run-agent.sh > agentwatch-kill.out 2>&1
grep -E '^DENIED|^open .*decoys' agentwatch-kill.out | head -5
tail -3 agentwatch-kill.out
```

```console
$ sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --kill -- ./run-agent.sh > agentwatch-kill.out 2>&1
$ grep -E '^DENIED|^open .*decoys' agentwatch-kill.out | head -5
$ tail -3 agentwatch-kill.out
```

The `cat` that opened the credentials is dead, and goose reports a failed step. That's enforcement of a kind, and it's how tools like Tetragon's `Sigkill` action work. Now look closely at what the kernel actually did, with `strace` on a bare `cat`:

```bash
sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --kill -- strace -e trace=openat,read -o strace.out cat decoys/.aws/credentials
tail -4 strace.out
```

```console
$ sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --kill -- strace -e trace=openat,read -o strace.out cat decoys/.aws/credentials
$ tail -4 strace.out
```

Look at the last `openat` line: it ends in `= ?`, and the next line is the kill. `strace` never saw the call return, because `bpf_send_signal` had already queued `SIGKILL` and it landed on the way back to userspace. The open itself was not refused; our tracepoint ran beside the syscall, not inside its permission check, so the kernel finished opening the file and only then delivered the signal. This `cat` lost the race by a hair. A program that already holds the descriptor, or one with a second thread reading, wins it. A kill is a reaction, and a reaction is a race.

To say no, the program has to run where the kernel asks permission. That's the LSM hook in `bpf/agentdeny.bpf.c`:

```c
SEC("lsm/file_open")
int BPF_PROG(deny_credential_open, struct file *file, int ret)
{
    if (ret || !in_scope())
        return ret;
    char path[PATH_MAX_BYTES] = {};
    long resolved = bpf_d_path((struct path *)&file->f_path, path, sizeof(path));
    if (resolved >= 0 && !is_credential_path(path))
        return 0;
    ...
    return -EPERM;
}
```

Same check, different place. `file_open` is the LSM hook that runs before any file is opened, `bpf_d_path` resolves the real path from the kernel's own `struct file` (so a relative path or a symlink can't dodge it), and returning `-EPERM` is the decision. The final `ret` argument preserves an earlier BPF LSM denial. An unresolved or overlong path also fails closed within this scope. `--deny` loads this alongside the watcher:

```bash
sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --deny -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials 2>&1 | grep -E '^cat:|lsm denied'
```

```console
cat: decoys/.aws/credentials: Operation not permitted
lsm denied 1 credential open(s)
```

No file descriptor, no bytes, no race. `cat` got `EPERM` from `openat` and printed the error you'd get from a permissions bit, and goose gets the same when you run the whole task under `--deny`. This is the difference between an eBPF program that observes and one that decides, and only the LSM attach point offers the second.

<details>
<summary>What the verifier rejected, the first time</summary>

The credential check scans the path for `/.aws/` with two nested loops. On older kernels the verifier refused any loop it couldn't unroll; since 5.3 it accepts a loop it can prove bounded, which these are (the outer loop stops at 250, and at the first NUL). If you change `PATH_MAX_BYTES` or the loop bounds and the load fails with a verifier log, that log is the verifier explaining exactly which instruction it couldn't prove safe. Read it top to bottom; it's long but it's not cryptic.

</details>

## Ship it as telemetry

_~5 min · Hands-on_

An event stream on a terminal is a demo. The same stream as OpenTelemetry log records is something a team can alert on. `telemetry.py` maps each event onto the [semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/): `process.pid`, `process.executable.name`, `file.path` for opens, `network.peer.address` and `network.peer.port` for connects, with `DENIED` events at `WARN`. Start a collector that prints everything it receives:

```bash
docker compose -f otel/compose.yaml up -d --wait
```

```console
$ docker compose -f otel/compose.yaml up -d --wait
```

Run the watcher with `--otlp`, then read the collector's log:

```bash
sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --otlp http://localhost:4318 -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
sleep 3
docker compose -f otel/compose.yaml logs collector > collector.log 2>&1
grep -B12 -A2 'decoys/.aws/credentials' collector.log | head -30
```

```console
$ sudo uv run python agentwatch.py --otlp http://localhost:4318 -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
$ sleep 3
$ docker compose -f otel/compose.yaml logs collector > collector.log 2>&1
$ grep -B12 -A2 'decoys/.aws/credentials' collector.log | head -30
```

One log record per kernel event, with the process and file facts as attributes any backend can filter on. Swap the `debug` exporter in `otel/collector.yaml` for an OTLP exporter and this is a feed into whatever you already run.

Question: if you were writing the first alert on this stream, what would it key on? Have a think, then open the answer 🤔

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`agentwatch.kind == "denied"` is the obvious one, and it's also the least useful: by the time it fires, the policy already did its job. The alert worth having is on `file.path` matching a credential location with `agentwatch.kind == "open"`, from a run *without* `--deny`, because that's a policy gap you didn't know about. Observe first, enforce second, alert on the difference. That ordering is exactly how Tetragon's observe-then-enforce policies are meant to be rolled out, which is the next lab.

</details>
